Many quantum tasks encode the answer in an eigenphase: an energy in Hamiltonian evolution, an order in modular arithmetic, or a probability in amplitude amplification. A phase is not directly visible in a computational-basis measurement. Phase estimation uses controlled evolution and interference to turn it into a classical binary record 

Cleve et al., 1998.

The quantum Fourier transform (QFT) combines the phases carried by a register. Phase estimation first prepares a superposition of different evolution lengths, then applies an inverse QFT so that matching phases add and mismatching phases cancel. QFT produces a quantum state; it does not return every entry of a classical Fourier transform in one measurement. This chapter supplies reusable components for the survey’s applications 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Implemented scope

Exact and truncated QFT, textbook QPE, one-ancilla feedback QPE, 

fresh-preparation Hadamard phase estimation, 

circular-grid Bayesian inference and 

bounded-bias robust inference have explicit circuits and independent small-instance checks. The Bayesian companion retains eight prescribed ideal-model transcripts; its credible grid-cell arcs do not supply a uniform confidence certificate or physical estimate. Robust inference supplies a conservative conditional guarantee under its independent-Bernoulli/additive-bias promise; experimental calibration and physical costing remain planned. Five static-QPE surface-code projections are computed under the audited conditional mean-fit model. A separate 

matched three/four-bit feedback comparison costs actual synthesized corrections, every branch’s common reserved schedule and the final classical median under a declared surface-code scenario. Eigenstate preparation for an arbitrary application and certified rotation synthesis remain application responsibilities. No integrated Lean proof is supplied.

For N=2^m, our positive-sign QFT convention isF_N\lvert x\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}\lvert y\rangle.

The circuit uses m Hadamards, m(m-1)/2 controlled-phase gates and \lfloor m/2\rfloor swaps. Wire q[0] is the least-significant bit. Swaps are included, so the matrix is the expression above rather than a bit-reversed variant. The inverse reverses the gate order and the phase signs.

QPE accepts an explicit n-qubit circuit U and an explicit preparation circuit for an eigenstateU\lvert\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}\lvert\psi\rangle,\qquad 0\leq\phi<1.

It prepares m phase qubits with Hadamards, applies controlled U^{2^j} from phase wire j, applies F_N^\dagger and measures those m wires. The decoded integer y estimates \phi by y/N. Our generator constructs each power from 2^j complete controlled calls to the supplied U; no power or dense matrix is treated as a free oracle. A supplied global phase becomes a conditional phase and is retained.

For an eigenstate, the independent reference distribution isP(y)=\frac{1}{N^2}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ik(\phi-y/N)}\right|^2.

A phase exactly on the grid is recovered with ideal probability one. For other phases, the two adjacent grid points are within circular error 1/N and together have probability at least 8/\pi^2. The median of 15 independent scalar estimates has majority-failure bound below 0.005 at that single-run bound. Scalar medians require \phi\in[1/N,1-1/N], so the good interval does not cross the phase branch cut. A circular median is not implemented. If the input is a superposition of eigenstates, the output is the corresponding phase mixture; a good phase-resolution bound does not establish overlap with the desired eigenstate.

Phase estimation is a family of measurement and inference procedures. The right choice depends on the requested output, the prepared state, available controlled evolution, coherent lifetime and classical processing. Our executed scope includes exact/truncated QFT, textbook QPE, 

retained-target feedback QPE, 

fresh-preparation Hadamard inference, 

bounded circular-grid Bayesian inference and 

bounded-bias robust inference. The remaining additional methods below are literature-backed implementation plans. Their papers and external software do not validate our circuits or physical resources. Each implemented variant retains its own stated input and evidence scope.

Family

Main change and suitable task

Costs and assumptions to retain

Book status

Coherent textbook QPE

A phase register and inverse QFT return a binary estimate of a sampled eigenphase 

Cleve et al., 1998.

Actual controlled powers, clock preparation, eigenstate weight, coherent synthesis and final readout.

Implemented with bounded ideal checks and conditional static surface-code projections.

Approximate QFT and semiclassical/iterative QPE

Truncated QFT omits small rotations. Semiclassical readout replaces measured Fourier interactions with feedback; one-ancilla iterative QPE reuses its clock 

Griffiths & Niu, 1996

Dobšíček et al., 2007.

Truncation error is part of the coherent budget. Clock reuse adds resets, feedback and retained-target exposure; it does not remove the controlled-power work.

Implemented ideal instrument and matched three/four-bit physical study; wider application, certified hardware confidence and physical size scaling remain planned.

Hadamard-test/Kitaev-style inference

Measure sine/cosine information from selected controlled powers, then unwrap or infer the phase classically. It avoids a coherent inverse QFT 

Cleve et al., 1998.

Power schedule, branch ambiguity, shots at every power and target preparations. A single fringe cannot identify a high-precision phase.

Implemented bounded repeated-access circuit and numerical recovery; physical costing and general application access remain planned.

Bayesian/adaptive inference

Update a circular phase distribution after each observation and choose later powers or measurement phases. Mixed-prior methods also address multiple spectral components 

Wiebe & Granade, 2016

Berg, 2021.

Likelihood/noise calibration, prior, classical update cost, maximum power and stopping rule. A posterior credible interval alone is not a uniform frequentist success guarantee.

Implemented fixed-length single-phase grid example, with complete fresh-trial accounting and bounded ideal checks. Noise calibration, mixed spectral inputs, stopping certificates and physical costing remain planned.

Robust phase estimation

Repeated sine/cosine experiments and phase unwrapping tolerate bounded probability distortions under an explicit model 

Kimmel et al., 2015.

The calibration/noise assumptions and corrected error analysis. The author’s 2021 version states that the original error-event analysis was incorrect and provides replacement references 

Kimmel et al., 2021. Robust inference is a different contract from full algorithm fault tolerance.

Implemented bounded readout-confusion example with exact circular recovery and an independently derived conservative conditional bound. Experimental calibration, rotation synthesis, physical estimates and reproduced formal proofs remain planned.

Statistical energy and multiple-eigenvalue estimation

Infer spectral information from many short Hadamard experiments rather than one large phase-register circuit. Lin–Tong estimates a spectral cumulative distribution and ground energy; QCELS fits complex exponentials; QMEGS targets several dominant eigenvalues 

Lin & Tong, 2022

Ding & Lin, 2023

Ding et al., 2024.

Ground/dominant weight, spectral interval and any gap/relative-overlap promise, all shots and classical fitting. QCELS’s smaller longest-time prefactor depends on overlap; QMEGS’s strongest depth reduction needs additional gap and state assumptions.

Planned application-specific companions to 

energy estimation.

Compressed-sensing spectral recovery

Recover a sparse spectral signal from a small set of discrete Hadamard-experiment times, using classical sparse recovery 

Yi et al., 2024.

Sparsity, approximately-on-grid and separation assumptions for the theorem; off-grid numerical tests have a different evidence scope. Charge all shots, controlled evolutions and classical optimization.

Planned; the inspected upstream experiments generate ideal spectral samples rather than compiled quantum circuits.

Randomized Fourier estimation with residual noise

Randomly sample powers and measurement quadratures, then identify the phase through a classical Fourier estimator 

Kshirsagar et al., 2024.

Bounded probability distortions or the paper’s Gaussian noise model, maximum power, dephasing scale and sample count. These assumptions differ from randomized Hamiltonian access.

Planned; use the February 13, 2025 corrected arXiv version, which fixes a sign in Equation 4 and Algorithm 1.

Circuit division and noise-aware likelihood estimation

Split the coherent demand across repeated QFT-based experiments; MSQPE and explicitly unbiased maximum-likelihood estimation trade residual noise against more samples 

Dutkiewicz et al., 2025.

Noise characterization, mitigation weights, likelihood regularization, overlap, repetitions and factory throughput. The external physical examples exclude good initial-state preparation.

Planned matched co-design comparison; the external surface-code estimates do not reprice this book’s baseline.

Randomized statistical Hamiltonian access

Wan–Berta–Campbell replaces exact evolution with an unbiased randomized estimator for spectral thresholding 

Wan et al., 2022.

Sampling the Hamiltonian terms, their coefficient norm, Pauli support and the sampling/precision tradeoff. Independence from the number of terms in an oracle-level bound does not eliminate input loading or compiled Pauli-string cost.

Planned comparison with explicit Hamiltonian access.

Partially randomized product-formula access

Keep a selected subset of Hamiltonian terms deterministic and sample the remaining terms within single-ancilla phase estimation 

Günther et al., 2026.

The partition and sampler, actual controlled term evolution at every power, stochastic and splitting errors, eigenstate preparation, all shots and classical inference.

Planned chemistry-access companion; the published resource estimates remain external.

Windowed QPE and energy filtering

Shape the clock amplitudes to control spectral leakage. DPSS/MPS preparation is a recent candidate for confidence windows; sine/Kaiser windows also support QPE-based filtering 

Kristjuhan & Berry, 2026

Sakuma et al., 2026.

Actual window preparation, its approximation error, the confidence objective, transition width and every rejected preparation. Classical postselected spectral data and a prepared quantum state are different outputs.

Planned window/preparation and filtering pages.

The 2026 DPSS paper reports that bond dimension four approximates the clock states for tested dimensions through 

224, and describes recycling three control qubits for power-of-two dimensions 

Kristjuhan & Berry, 2026. This is a useful preparation and feedback co-design candidate. Its numerical approximation coverage is not a uniform certificate for every future generated window or physical implementation.

Günther and colleagues’ partially randomized method changes the
Hamiltonian-simulation subroutine inside single-ancilla phase estimation


Günther et al., 2026. The published chemistry resource
estimates motivate a new access implementation. They do not establish a
matched physical improvement for our repeated-phase-gate examples; that
comparison needs the same Hamiltonian, output accuracy, prepared-state
promise, confidence and hardware assumptions.

For an eigenphase U|\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}|\psi\rangle, a Hadamard experiment with controlled U^k and a phase offset \beta has\Pr(0\mid k,\beta)=\tfrac12\left[1+\operatorname{Re}\!\left(e^{-i\beta}\langle\psi|U^k|\psi\rangle\right)\right].

Offsets 0 and \pi/2 reveal cosine and sine information. For a mixed spectral input the signal is a weighted sum of eigenphases, rather than one unknown scalar phase. Retaining the target through a measurement sequence and freshly preparing it for every experiment have different joint distributions. The 

retained-target energy confidence protocol cannot be transferred to a fresh-preparation sampler without a new argument.

For experiments at Hamiltonian times t_j, with N_j shots, record bothT_{\max}=\max_j|t_j|,\qquad
T_{\mathrm{evol}}=\sum_jN_j|t_j|,

and charge every preparation, actual controlled evolution, synthesis allocation, measurement, reset/feedback and classical fit. T_{\max} measures the longest evolution demand; T_{\mathrm{evol}} measures accumulated evolution work. Neither equals physical wall time without compiling the gates and accounting for code cycles, factories, repeated initialization and scheduling. A lower coherent depth can require more shots. Compare variants at the same requested output, accuracy, success, initial-state promise and frozen physical assumptions.

Qualtran’s pinned textbook QPE supplies decomposition and compositional counts under Apache-2.0. Its 

Kaiser-window class supplies coefficients, tensor semantics and a resource call graph; that class does not itself provide a preparation-circuit decomposition. A window vector is insufficient evidence of its compiled cost.

Phayes (Apache-2.0) and 

Sandia pyRPE (BSD-3-Clause/Apache-2.0 options) are classical inference candidates. The quantum experiment and reproducible environment remain our responsibilities. The 

QCELS/QMEGS comparison repository is a reference: the inspected code draws ideal samples from supplied eigenvalues/populations, and no license was found. We have not adopted its code or dependencies.

The

It pins several direct dependencies, including Qualtran 0.4.1, but has no complete transitive environment lock and does not export a complete MSQPE circuit. We have not installed or reproduced it. An exact m-wire Fourier circuit has quadratic controlled-phase count. Its longest-range phases are exponentially small. Omitting those phases reduces gate construction and eventual synthesis work at a declared coherent approximation cost, following the approximate-transform idea of Coppersmith 

Coppersmith, 1994.

build_qft(m, max_distance=b) retains the Hadamards and final swaps, and keeps only controlled phases with wire separation d\leq b. A retained gate has angle \pi/2^d. The retained count is \sum_{d=1}^{b}(m-d), giving O(mb) controlled phases rather than O(m^2). Setting b=m-1 is the exact circuit; b=0 retains only Hadamards and swaps.

For an omitted phase \theta, \|CP(\theta)-I\|_2=2|\sin(\theta/2)|\leq|\theta|. A telescoping product of unitary gates therefore gives the original bound\|\widetilde F_N-F_N\|_2\leq
\min\!\left(2,\sum_{d=b+1}^{m-1}(m-d)\frac{\pi}{2^d}\right)
\leq\min(2,\pi m/2^b).

The inverse has the same bound. Choosing b\geq\lceil\log_2(\pi m/\eta)\rceil, capped at m-1, meets a sufficient spectral-norm omission allowance \eta. This bound covers the omitted ideal phases. It does not cover inaccuracies in retained rotations, physical faults or application readout confidence.

For an exact prepared eigenstate U|\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}|\psi\rangle, an H–controlled-U^k–H experiment givesp_{\cos}(0)=\tfrac12[1+\cos(2\pi k\phi)].

Applying S^\dagger to the control before the final H instead givesp_{\sin}(0)=\tfrac12[1+\sin(2\pi k\phi)].

The implementation uses k_j=2^j, j=0,\ldots,L-1, and m independent fresh trials per basis and power. From the zero counts, construct c_j=2\widehat p_{\cos,j}-1, s_j=2\widehat p_{\sin,j}-1, and \theta_j=\operatorname{atan2}(s_j,c_j)/(2\pi)\bmod1. Start with \widehat\phi_0=\theta_0; at each later power choose the circular lift (\theta_j+r)/k_j nearest the preceding estimate. A zero empirical signal returns explicit ambiguity.

This is the specified dyadic recovery protocol, rather than a claim to implement every published Kitaev, Bayesian or robust estimator. Recovery receives only counts, powers and shot totals; it receives no true phase or eigenvalue. A non-eigenstate instead yields a weighted spectral signal, which need not lie on the unit circle. The single-phase argument does not cover such inputs. Freshly preparing a mixed state for every experiment also differs from the 

retained-target feedback instrument and the energy chapter’s retained-target median protocol.

If both estimated probabilities at one power differ from their ideal values by at most 1/8, the complex-signal error is at most \sqrt2/4. Its phase-angle error is therefore smaller than 1/8 cycles. The correct next lift lies within 3/(8k_j) of the preceding estimate, strictly inside half the lift spacing; induction gives circular phase error at most\epsilon_\phi=\frac1{8k_{\max}}=2^{-(L+2)}.

Hoeffding for the 2L proportions and a union bound give\Pr(\text{failure})\le4L\exp(-m/32).

The shot planner uses an exact positive rational Taylor lower bound on \exp(m/32), so its reciprocal is a conservative upper bound. The integer threshold is not selected by a rounded logarithm alone. The finite-degree planner is conservative; it may choose additional shots or reject extreme requests, and is not claimed globally optimal for the exact exponential law. This arithmetic bound assumes exact eigenstate preparation, exact controlled powers, IID fresh ideal trials and exact-real angular inference. It does not certify our floating-point atan2, circuit realization, synthesis or noisy hardware.

Repeated interference experiments can identify an eigenphase even when the measurement probabilities have a bounded systematic distortion. A long controlled evolution magnifies a small phase difference; sine and cosine observations identify its circular angle, and shorter evolutions identify the correct alias. This is the robust phase-estimation idea used in gate calibration 

Kimmel et al., 2015.

Implemented scope

This companion supplies original explicit fresh-preparation circuits, rational circular inference, a seeded small readout-confusion example and logical scaling. It uses an independently derived conservative finite-sample guarantee. The 2015 paper’s original error analysis is not adopted. Circuits and readout laws are checked numerically; the arithmetic confidence argument is mathematical and is not a reproduced formal proof. Physical estimation and experimental calibration remain planned.

executed nine-wire primitive export and retained failed/succeeded generation

source counts supply no phase result, synthesis certificate or physical estimate.

The input is an exactly prepared single eigenstateU|\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}|\psi\rangle,\qquad\phi\in[0,1).

At each power k_j=2^j, j=0,\ldots,L-1, use m fresh independent trials in each of two quadratures. The ideal zero probabilities arep_{c,j}=\tfrac12[1+\cos(2\pi k_j\phi)],\qquad
p_{s,j}=\tfrac12[1+\sin(2\pi k_j\phi)].

Our probability model specifies an actual Bernoulli probability q_{b,j} for each batch, with|q_{b,j}-p_{b,j}|\le\beta<\tfrac18.

Trials are independent and identically distributed within each batch. A single bias bound must hold at every chosen power and quadrature; it may have different signs in different batches. The bound is supplied as an input promise. No experiment estimates it here. State-preparation, controlled-evolution or synthesis errors can enter this contract only after proving that their combined effect satisfies the probability bound. Correlated drift, arbitrary mixed spectral inputs and unbounded power-dependent dephasing are outside this single-phase guarantee.

With zero counts z_{c,j},z_{s,j}, construct the exact rational signalsc_j=2z_{c,j}/m-1,\qquad s_j=2z_{s,j}/m-1.

The code encloses \operatorname{atan2}(s_j,c_j)/(2\pi)\bmod1 in an exact rational interval [a_j,b_j] and uses its midpoint \widetilde\theta_j. It begins with \widehat\phi_0=\widetilde\theta_0. At power k_j>1, choose a lift (\widetilde\theta_j+\ell)/k_j nearest the preceding circular estimate. Every interval decision uses fractions. In particular, accept an integer \ell only if\ell-\tfrac12<k_j\widehat\phi_{j-1}-b_j
\quad\text{and}\quad
k_j\widehat\phi_{j-1}-a_j<\ell+\tfrac12.

This ensures that the same lift is nearest for every angle in the enclosure. Normalize the lifted midpoint modulo one. Zero signal, an enclosure outside its width guard or a half-spacing boundary returns an explicit inconclusive result, retaining all counts and completed decisions. An accepted result does not itself verify the unknown bias promise.

Set t=1/8-\beta>0. Hoeffding applied to each of the 2L empirical proportions gives\Pr(\text{some }|\widehat p_{b,j}-q_{b,j}|>t)
\le4L\exp(-2mt^2).

On the complementary event, each empirical signal component differs from its ideal value by at most 2(\beta+t)=1/4. The complex-signal error is at most \sqrt2/4. Tangent geometry around the unit circle gives an angular error smaller than 1/16 turn, since\sqrt2/4<\sin(\pi/8).

The code requires an angle-enclosure width at most 1/96 turn. Its midpoint therefore adds at most 1/192 turn, giving a fringe-center error below 13/192<r=1/12. The correct next lift is at distance at most 3r/k_j from the preceding estimate: the preceding error contributes 2r/k_j, and the new center contributes r/k_j. Because 3r=1/4<1/2, the correct lift is unique. The enclosure width also leaves a strict margin for the interval decision above. Induction yieldsd_{\mathbb T}(\widehat\phi,\phi)\le\epsilon_\phi
=\frac1{12\,2^{L-1}}

except on an event of probability at most 4L\exp(-2mt^2). Inconclusive outputs belong to that failure event; they are never omitted from a reported study. The returned closed circular arc splits into two rational intervals when it crosses zero. This is a conditional uniform coverage argument over the stated probability model, not a Bayesian credible interval or an empirical coverage estimate.

The planner uses the positive 128-term rational Taylor sum E_{128}(2mt^2)\le\exp(2mt^2) and accepts a shot count only when\frac{4L}{E_{128}(2mt^2)}\le\delta.

All ceiling comparisons are exact. The finite-degree bound can be conservative and the finite trial cap can reject a request; the planner does not claim the globally optimal shot count. The angle calculation uses a 32-term alternating arctangent series with its signed next-term remainder, an exact range reduction to magnitude at most 1/2, and Machin’s identity \pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239). Axes and quadrant decisions are exact. No floating-point atan2 determines an alias.

A classical random walk adds probabilities along possible routes. A quantum walk propagates amplitudes, so routes can reinforce or cancel when they meet. A coin supplies the direction register for a discrete walk; continuous-time walks instead evolve under a graph Hamiltonian. Quantum walks are useful primitives in search, sampling and quantum simulation, but their graph access, preparation and output requirements determine an application’s cost 

Aharonov et al., 2001.

This chapter implements a Hadamard-coin walk on a cycle. Separate method pages implement 

SKW-style marked-hypercube search with an actual equality oracle and 

continuous-time hypercube dynamics. Their graphs, evolution and output contracts differ; the resource plots are not an equal-task advantage comparison.

Implemented scope

Binary carry gates implement the coin-controlled cycle shifts. Small circuits are checked against independent permutation matrices and amplitude recurrences. Complete measured circuits, source code, size sweeps and conditional surface-code reports are supplied. No dense shift/evolution matrix constructs a quantum gate. The 

bounded SKW search separately checks its joint marked-state reflection, clean workspace and literal Clifford+T sequence. General graph access, other marked-search families, Szegedy walks, certified arbitrary-rotation synthesis and an integrated Lean proof remain further implementations.

Encode N=2^n positions in n bits and use one coin qubit. A step isU=S(H_c\otimes I),\qquad
S|c,x\rangle=|c,x+(2c-1)\bmod N\rangle.

Chronologically apply the Hadamard to the coin, then shift. Coin zero moves left; coin one moves right. The coin occupies wire q[n], and q[0] is the least significant position bit. The n=1 case has coincident left/right neighbors and is a degenerate two-vertex example; the main sweep starts at n=2.

The displayed input is position zero and coin (|0\rangle+i|1\rangle)/\sqrt2, prepared by H then S. Other implemented inputs are basis positions and coin zero or one. The output contract is one return-event probability after a stated number of steps. Every complete trial measures all position and coin wires. Classical decoding ignores every coin outcome and checks whether the position equals its start; it never postselects a coin value. A full histogram is a bounded illustration, not the same precision contract.

For a conditional increment, visit the position bits from high to low: flip bit j when the coin and all lower bits are one, then flip bit zero under the coin. This implements binary carry without scratch wires. Reversing that sequence implements decrement. Sandwich the decrement with coin X gates to control it on zero. Both coin branches are coherent and their relative phase is retained.

One step has 2n+3 source instructions: 2n controlled carry flips, two coin X gates and one coin Hadamard. Multi-controlled flips are subsequently decomposed. Let C_j denote the implemented primitive cost of an X with j controls. The actual shift costs 2\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_j+2 plus the coin gate; it is not a constant-cost neighbor oracle. With T steps, add input preparation, T complete shifts/coins and n+1 final measurements. Width is n+1, with zero scratch ancillas. The compiled CSV records the cost of the pinned compiler instead of assigning every MCX unit cost.

The

The classical walk is a comparator; the independent quantum permutation/recurrence is the correctness check. This finite bipartite cycle has parity restrictions, so neither curve should be interpreted as ordinary fixed-time convergence to a uniform distribution.

A continuous-time walk spreads amplitudes by evolving under a graph’s adjacency Hamiltonian. On the n-dimensional hypercube, a vertex is an n-bit string and each edge flips one bit. The adjacency therefore has a particularly simple representation: a sum of Pauli X operators. The terms commute, so every coordinate evolves independently. This supplies a transparent companion to the 

coined cycle walk, whose coin and conditional shifts generate different interference.

Hypercube walks and their mixing behavior are studied by Moore and Russell 

Moore & Russell, 2002. Our explicit convention below fixes the edge weight and time units. This special factorization is also easy to simulate classically; it establishes no quantum advantage or generic graph-access implementation.

Set \hbar=1 and specifyH=J\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}X_q,\qquad U(t)=e^{-iHt}.

The classical input is the register width n, coupling J, time t, and starting vertex x. Prepare |x\rangle with one X gate per set bit.

Here J specifies the energy scale and t is in inverse-energy units with \hbar=1. This model-evolution time is separate from the physical duration of the compiled gate circuit. Since distinct-coordinate Pauli terms commute,U(t)=\bigotimes_{q=0}^{n-1}\left(\cos(Jt)I-i\sin(Jt)X\right)
=\prod_{q=0}^{n-1}R_X(2Jt).

The circuit constructs these actual rotations. It does not append a dense matrix exponential or load graph eigenvectors. Basis state preparation is explicit; arbitrary amplitude loading is outside this example.

For a destination y, let h=\operatorname{popcount}(x\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}y). The analytic probability isP(y,t)=\sin^{2h}(Jt)\cos^{2(n-h)}(Jt),\qquad P(x,t)=\cos^{2n}(Jt).

At |Jt|=\pi/4, all 2^n vertices have probability 2^{-n}. At Jt=\pi/2, the walk reaches the bitwise antipode with amplitude (-i)^n. Global phases matter for a coherently controlled evolution: at Jt=\pi, U=(-1)^nI, not always I.

The graph’s degree is n. Choosing normalized adjacency means J=1/n, so the uniform-time value becomes t=\pi n/4. Choosing J=1 instead gives t=\pi/4. Times from differently normalized models must not be compared directly.

The canonical generated example has n=3, J=1, t=.7 and x=000. Its unitary consists of three RX rotations; the complete measured trial adds all three position readouts. The notebook separately checks the uniform distribution at t=\pi/4, where the return probability is 1/8.

For one trial, logical space is n qubits. Input preparation uses \operatorname{popcount}(x) X gates, evolution uses n RX gates for nonzero represented Jt, and complete position readout uses n measurements. Factoring an integer becomes easier if we know the period of its modular powers. Shor’s algorithm uses interference to reveal that period: a superposition of exponents is entangled with a^x\bmod N, and an inverse Fourier transform makes samples concentrate near multiples of the reciprocal order 

Shor, 1997. The classical gcd step turns suitable periods into factors. The survey discusses the application and its full resource context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Implementation status

The N=15 and N=21 examples execute actual modular-add and modular-multiply circuits, with numerical checks against independent classical answers. The parameterized generator constructs gates without an arithmetic lookup table or a dense unitary matrix. Logical scaling is measured separately from the bounded simulations. The default Fourier projection is joined by eight matched Fourier/ripple surface-code reports for four-, five-, and six-bit workloads. These use the audited QDK mean synthesis-cost model; they do not supply certified Clifford+T approximations or a general factoring benchmark. The 

measured-AND companion adds an executed ideal measurement-assisted replacement, bounded addition/order checks and materialized logical scaling; its physical comparison and mechanized proof remain pending.

Given N and a chosen base a with \gcd(a,N)=1, the order is the smallest positive r satisfying a^r\equiv1\pmod N. If a verified period is even, let b=a^{r/2}\bmod N. Nontrivial values of \gcd(b-1,N) and \gcd(b+1,N) give factors. Odd periods and b=\pm1 can fail, so they must not disappear from success accounting.

Our input is the classical pair (N,a). It specifies ordinary gate constants and the bit width n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil; there is no external database or amplitude-loading oracle. The work register begins at 1, while the t exponent qubits begin in a uniform superposition. Controlled multiplication by a^{2^j}\bmod N entangles the jth exponent bit with the modular-power register. All work ancillas are uncomputed before the inverse QFT and exponent readout.

The arithmetic follows Fourier addition and compute–swap–uncompute multiplication 

Draper, 2000

Beauregard, 2003, using an original Qiskit 2.6.2 implementation. Qiskit is Apache-2.0 software; see its 

upstream repository and our 

MIT implementation.

For 0\le y<N, a modular addition uses an (n+1)-bit accumulator and one borrow flag. In the Fourier basis it adds a constant c, subtracts N, conditionally restores N after inspecting the high bit, and removes the borrow information using the relation between the result and c. QFTs, controlled phase gates, X gates and CX gates implement every step. Addition by c is controlled; the subtract/restore work cancels on inactive control branches. The accumulator’s high bit and borrow flag return to zero.

To multiply by a, add a2^j\bmod N into a zero accumulator, controlled by each input bit. Swap the input with the result under the exponent control. Then subtract the binary-weighted multiples of a^{-1}\bmod N controlled by the new input bits. The old input is erased because a^{-1}(ax\bmod N)\equiv x\pmod N. This includes the inverse arithmetic, rather than charging an opaque modular-multiplication box.

The contract requires x<N, a zero accumulator and a clean flag. Outside that subspace the same gate circuit remains reversible, but we assign it no modular-arithmetic meaning. All QFT angles are numerical representations of exact analytic angles; fault-tolerant synthesis is a separate layer.

In-memory arithmetic preserves the relative phases needed for coherent controls. The pinned QASM exporter omits the compiled circuit’s overall global phase, recorded in the ledger. Our QASM files describe complete measured trials with unchanged probabilities; they are not specifications for a phase-preserving oracle to be coherently controlled again.

Regev’s published algorithm uses approximately \sqrt n independent quantum executions, each with a gate count of order n^{3/2} up to logarithmic factors, followed by classical lattice processing. Its correctness relies on a number-theoretic conjecture, and the paper explicitly leaves practical physical improvement unresolved 

Regev, 2025. The gate count is per execution: the repetitions and classical lattice work must remain in the total cost.

Ragavan and Vaikuntanathan reduce the quantum workspace while keeping the smaller per-run circuit and make classical recovery tolerate a constant fraction of corrupted runs 

Ragavan & Vaikuntanathan, 2026. The inspected associated manuscript states  O(n\log n) qubits and  O(n^{3/2}\log n) gates per run, with  O(\sqrt n) runs. These asymptotic statements use the papers’ arithmetic model, rather than the current book generator’s simple cubic arithmetic. Tolerance of corrupted samples is a recovery property; a physical implementation still needs error correction, synthesis and a failure budget.

This deserves a separate planned page beneath the factoring chapter when we implement it. That page should show a small multidimensional exponentiation circuit, actual lattice recovery, the number-theoretic assumption, and a comparison with the same factoring/output/success task. No Regev circuit or physical estimate is implemented here yet.

Total logical work is R times the complete trial count. The measured toy values of p must not be extrapolated to arbitrary integers.

The table selects the fewest-qubit and fastest-model Pareto choices separately; the 

CSV records both. Peak qubits multiplied by serial model time is their reported product, rather than an integral of active qubits over time. The full reports retain source dependency depth, canonical rotation/T counts, synthesis allocation, code distance, factories and all Pareto points.

The primary series supplies three bounded size points under a declared input and precision policy. Orders and identity powers differ across integers, and N15 has especially favorable identity multipliers. Ripple has more logical wires and compiled Boolean work; the declared model favors its lower arbitrary-rotation workload here. QDK reduces the circuit to canonical non-Clifford/measurement counts on placeholder wires, and PSSPC does not preserve the actual Clifford dependency graph. The projected times therefore remain conditional on that abstraction; the study is neither a universal physical scaling fit nor a classical factoring benchmark.

The old circuit-materialization control N=33,a=2,t=12 is retained with zero ideal factor success and no finite-retry physical factoring projection. Its order is ten and 2^5\equiv-1\pmod{33}, so the verified-period gcd rule cannot return a nontrivial factor. More precision or retries cannot repair that base. Its actual circuits and logical counts remain available in the study, with the unsupported retry contract labeled explicitly.

Every trial includes input-1 and exponent preparation, controlled modular powers, accumulator/constant/carry/borrow handling, inverse arithmetic, inverse QFT and all exponent measurements. Serial executions assume fresh logical-zero inputs. Calibrated physical initialization/reset, external I/O, classical constant construction and CF/gcd verification latency, routing and decoder timing are excluded from the physical clock; diagnostic work and wall times are separate. These fixed-base reports do not project the combined success, stopping behavior or runtime of the adaptive random-base or recursive 

factoring driver.

The Gidney–Ekerå construction is a useful external end-to-end reference: it combines optimized arithmetic and recovery with a surface-code layout, magic-state factories, repeated attempts and a specified controller reaction time 

Gidney & Ekerå, 2021. Its RSA-2048 estimate uses 20 million noisy qubits and an expected eight-hour runtime under a particular nearest-neighbor hardware model. Those numbers are not extrapolations from our N15/N21 circuits.

A later Gidney preprint trades more time for less space, using approximate residue arithmetic, dense idle storage and smaller magic-state production. Its headline estimate is below a million noisy qubits and below a week, with the same stated physical error, cycle and controller assumptions as the earlier reference 

Gidney, 2025. The paper’s dense-storage choice uses yoked surface codes, whose published memory results concern a hierarchical code over a nearest-neighbor square grid 

Gidney et al., 2025. A lower memory cost is not automatically a faster complete algorithm: transfers between storage and computation, factory throughput, arithmetic retries and controller latency still matter.

We will treat these as external conditional resource models, not as validated improvements to this book’s frozen baseline. A matched co-design comparison must hold the factoring problem, accepted input class, output, total failure probability and hardware assumptions fixed, and report physical qubits, runtime and spacetime volume. A new code or memory architecture also needs its own noise, operation and scheduling model.

The 2025 paper’s 

Zenodo code-and-assets record is an exact upstream starting point. The inspected record has a 6,220,929-byte code.zip and a CC-BY-4.0 license. We have inspected the record metadata, not executed that archive. The 2021 arXiv source separately provides estimate_costs.py and related ancillary files.

The November 2026 shared-lookup preprint provides a further arithmetic candidate and an 

exact supporting archive, whose metadata declares CC-BY-4.0 

Sharma & Lau, 2026. We inspected the manuscript and archive metadata, not the archive’s executable source. Its comparisons bind logical-qubit budgets and reference-simulator counts; wider shared lookup words can change the runtime benefit on another architecture. Neither its gate reductions nor its conditional timing transfers are a reproduced improvement to our frozen factoring workload.

The dedicated tests check positive-exponent QFT matrices, modular addition over valid basis inputs and active/inactive controls, multiplier semantics, auxiliary cleanup, coherent relative phases and decomposition. Full N=15 and N=21 phase marginals are compared with an independently evaluated Fourier sum over residue classes. This tests the actual circuit, rather than constructing a reference arithmetic matrix and calling it an implementation.

An independent review additionally checked 1,743 modular-adder branches and 102 multiplier branches through N=21, with full complex-amplitude discrepancies below 4\times10^{-14}. Numerical tests cover the stated bounded inputs; they are not a proof for every width.

A successful fixed-base order measurement is only one part of factoring. A driver must also recognize easy classical cases, choose bases, retain failed measurements, verify proposed factors and stop honestly when its budget is spent. This page implements that full control flow for bounded inputs, using the actual modular arithmetic from the 

main chapter.

Status and output contract

The driver returns a verified nontrivial factor split, an exact bounded prime classification, or an explicit failure/resource limit. A recursive wrapper continues splits until all factors are prime or some components remain unresolved. The circuits and traces below are executed ideal simulations; no generic factoring confidence theorem or adaptive fault-tolerant projection is supplied.

All inputs are integers 2\le N\le4095. The driver checks small primes, even inputs and exact perfect powers using integer roots. It then uses a deterministic two-base Miller–Rabin implementation in this bounded domain. The dedicated tests compare every input in the domain against an independent sieve; this is not an unbounded primality claim. Strong-pseudoprime tests provide the broader context 

Jaeschke, 1993.

For an odd composite that survives these checks, bases are drawn uniformly with replacement from 2,\ldots,N-1 using a recorded NumPy seed. A nontrivial \gcd(a,N) is an immediate classical factor. Coprime bases receive a bounded number of complete quantum trials. Every outcome is processed by continued fractions, checked with a^d\bmod N, and followed by gcd factor verification. The driver never enumerates the order to construct a circuit, sample a result or decide when to stop.

The semiclassical inverse Fourier transform replaces the exponent register with one measured and recycled control qubit 

Griffiths & Niu, 1996. Our original Qiskit 2.6.2 implementation uses actual reset, measurement and classical if_test operations. Qiskit is Apache-2.0 software; 

upstream is credited separately from our MIT code.

At output bit i=0,\ldots,t-1, apply H, controlled multiplication by a^{2^{t-1-i}}\bmod N, and the feedback phasesP\!\left(-\frac{\pi b_j}{2^{i-j}}\right),\qquad j<i,

where b_j is a previous measured bit. Apply H and measure b_i, then reset the control before the next step. The output integer is y=\sum_i b_i2^i, so bits arrive least significant first. All registers reset and the modular-power register is prepared at one at the beginning of each trial. Accumulator and borrow work is uncomputed on every branch.

The recursive wrapper verifies a prime/unresolved-product invariant throughout. Let B be the maximum base draws, S the trials allowed per coprime base and K the global quantum-trial cap. The driver follows all three caps, including cases where K<BS. We provide a separate numerical ideal-policy audit for N\le63 using an independent reference distribution; the actual driver does not call that reference.

For b remaining bases and q remaining quantum trials, the audit averages failures over all coprime bases. A noncoprime base contributes zero failure. For a coprime base with ideal success p_a, use u=\min(S,q) trials; its failure contribution is (1-p_a)^u times continuation F(b-1,q-S) when q\ge S, or a terminal failure when q<S. Also F(0,q)=1. A cap reached between bases still permits the next base’s classical gcd check; a cap reached inside a base terminates that run. This distinction is tested against independent finite-policy enumeration.

A temporary logical AND stores a predicate in a clean helper qubit. It can be
cheaper to compute that predicate, use it, and erase it by measurement than to
reverse its non-Clifford circuit. Gidney introduced this route for quantum
addition 

Gidney, 2018.

Measurement does not have to destroy the data coherence. Measuring the helper
in the X basis adds a known conditional phase to the data; a Clifford CZ
correction removes that phase. The helper’s measured value also tells us
whether an X is needed to return it to zero.

Executed ideal-circuit checkpoint

The dedicated module tests passed 109 cases. The generator executed six
bounded addition checks and two small order-finding checks, and the companion
notebook executed all seven code cells in a genuine Jupyter kernel, including
its circuit figure. The 

validation summary
records exact source and artifact hashes. Larger circuit exports remain
generation-only. No physical estimate, hardware execution or mechanized proof
is claimed.

For data controls a,b and a clean helper h, our literal computation isH(h), T(h), CX(b,h), Tdg(h), CX(a,h), T(h),
CX(b,h), Tdg(h), H(h), Sdg(h).

The first nine gates are a four-T relative-phase construction. On clean-helper
inputs its |11,0> branch has phase i; the final Sdg removes that phase, giving
|a,b,0> → |a,b,a∧b>. No claim is made that this computation is an exact CCX on
dirty-helper inputs.

Copy the predicate into an arbitrary data target with CX(h,target), apply
H(h), and measure h into m. The two uncorrected data Kraus operators are

[
K_m=2^{-1/2},CZ(a,b)^m,CCX(a,b,target).
]

Applying CZ iff m=1 makes both corrected branches CCX/√2. The data channel is
therefore exactly CCX in the ideal gate model, including coherent inputs and
entanglement with other registers. Applying X(h) iff m=1 clears the measured
helper without a second measurement. A separate literal-reset variant is
provided for comparison. Each lifetime keeps a and b unchanged until its
correction completes.

Our 

ripple baseline has 2w CCX and 4w CX gates before
lowering. Replacing each CCX gives 8w literal T/Tdg gates, compared with
14w for the standard seven-T decomposition. This is an unoptimized MAJ/UMA
drop-in variant, not Gidney’s separately optimized 4w−4 adder. Measurements,
helper storage and controller delays remain costs.

measurement outcomes and coherent data states. They compare the actual
primitive circuit’s Kraus operators with an independent classical CCX
permutation. Addition checks use independent integer arithmetic and coherent
permutation references. The small default is two-bit addition 3+1 modulo 4,
with carry-in zero; the first input and carry must be restored.

An order-finding measurement can encode a reduced fraction: its denominator
may omit a common factor of the unknown order. Extra classical processing can
recover that missing component without rerunning the quantum circuit. Ekerå’s
analysis combines a nearby-frequency search with a small-prime-power search


Ekerå, 2024. This page implements a bounded
continued-fraction route and makes its classical work visible.

Executed scope and the small-instance limit

The implementation uses original integer-only code, freshly checked arithmetic
circuits, identical samples for both recovery rules, and an additional bounded
exact-order certificate. It has no true-order oracle or input-factorization
routine. All default orders are small and fully smooth for the chosen
bound. The retained classical shortcut can recover them before using the
frequency; these examples demonstrate control flow and verification, not
quantum advantage. Physical costing and formal correspondence remain pending.

Let a be coprime to N, with unknown order r<2^m, and let t be the
number of measured phase bits. The implemented candidate route follows the
paper’s continued-fraction method and Algorithms 3 and 4:

Examine every distinct frequency j+u\pmod{2^t} for
u=0,+1,-1,\ldots,+B,-B. There is no early peak-isolation heuristic.

For each frequency, compute the last continued-fraction denominator q
with q^2<2^t, using exact integer comparisons. Retain 1\le q<2^m.

Set b=cm and
E=\prod_{p\le b}p^{\lfloor\log_p b\rfloor} over primes p.
The code constructs the powers by integer multiplication, avoiding rounded
logarithms. Keep candidates with a^{Eq}\equiv1\pmod N.

Algorithm 3 uses a product tree to isolate each prime-power component of
a^q, then finds its required exponent within the bound. Complete every
retained candidate and choose the smallest returned period.

Here b-smooth means each entire prime power is at most b. An order
component 16 is not 5-smooth, even though its only prime is two. The
implementation also retains the paper’s useful shortcut: if a^E=1, apply
Algorithm 3 to candidate one and recover the wholly smooth order classically.

For an optimal nearby frequency, the CF route requires t=m+l with
1\le l\le m and r^2<2^t. If its missing component is cm-smooth,
the good candidate produces r. An arbitrary candidate can instead produce
\operatorname{lcm}(r,q), a proper multiple of the order. The implementation
therefore distinguishes a verified period from an exact order. The lattice
variants and the complete general success bound are external references,
rather than implemented claims for every configured input


Ekerå, 2024.

periods remain labeled verified_period_only. This extra certificate does
not make arbitrary large-period factorization efficient.

The 

factoring circuit needs reversible modular multiplication. Fourier arithmetic stores addition in phases; ripple arithmetic carries ordinary binary information along a register using reversible Boolean gates. This variant makes the tradeoff visible: more work qubits and compiled operations, but many fewer general-angle rotations in the demonstrated circuits.

Implementation status

The carry, modular-add and modular-multiply circuits are implemented and numerically checked. The full N=15 and N=21 circuits are simulated with a bounded complex-amplitude source simulator. Small coherent circuits are independently checked with Qiskit. Larger generators and their logical counts are separate from quantum simulation. Physical results below are an equal-task conditional QDK model comparison, not an observed hardware speedup or a synthesis certificate.

Our original implementation uses the MAJ/UMA idea of Cuccaro, Draper, Kutin and Moulton 

Cuccaro et al., 2004. For bit wires (a,b,c), MAJ applies CX from a to b, CX from a to c, and CCX from (b,c) to a. The final a stores the majority/carry. Reverse UMA restores a and c while replacing b with their sum bit. Chaining MAJ from low to high bits and UMA in reverse gives|a,b,c\rangle\longmapsto |a,(a+b+c)\bmod 2^m,c\rangle.

The circuit exposes no overflow output. It uses 2m+1 wires, 2m Toffoli gates and 4m CX gates, with depth linear in m. These intentionally simple endpoints are not the paper’s optimized gate count.

records.content:
Let n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil and m=n+1. A constant addition prepares the constant into an m-bit zero register, runs the carry adder, then unprepares the restored constant register. Preparation uses X, CX or CCX for zero, one or two external controls. The adder itself remains an explicitly defined Boolean circuit.

A modular addition first adds b, subtracts N, copies the accumulator’s high bit into a borrow flag, and conditionally restores N. Subtracting b reveals the complementary sign condition needed to erase the flag; adding b restores the final result. The carry and constant register are clean after every addition. The subtract/restore work also cancels on an inactive control branch.

To multiply, add (a2^j\bmod N) for each input bit into a zero accumulator, swap the input/result under the external control, then subtract the inverse multiplier’s weighted constants to erase the old input. The circuit includes every control, constant preparation, swap and uncomputation. No dense unitary or arithmetic lookup table constructs a gate.

The valid contract is x<N, zero accumulator, borrow, constant and carry workspace. The same reversible circuit has an unspecified extension on invalid or dirty inputs. In-memory gates preserve the relative phases needed for coherent controls. Fully measured QASM exports omit the compiled overall global phase, recorded in their ledger; they are not phase-preserving specifications for another controlled oracle.

A product formula’s short alternating evolutions introduce commutator errors.
A corrector rotates the computational frame around that formula to cancel a
selected leading error. A symplectic corrector has an inverse on its other
side, so equal intermediate boundary operations cancel over a fixed sequence.
The remaining first and last operations still cost gates.

This page selects the first symplectic correction to Strang splitting from
Bagherimehrab and colleagues 

Bagherimehrab et al., 2026. The model
has disjoint two-spin pairs: it is classically factorized and provides a
transparent circuit check, with no application-advantage claim.

For m pairs and n=2m wires, defineA=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_jZ_{2j}Z_{2j+1},\qquad
B_0=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_jX_{2j},\qquad H=A+\alpha B_0.

The rational inputs have 0\le\alpha\le1, |a_j|,|b_j|\le4 and |t|\le4.
The energy unit and \hbar=1 fix the meaning of t. The known input uses H
on every wire and S on each lower pair wire, giving
|+y\rangle_{2j}|+\rangle_{2j+1}. The measured output is the Z_0 mean;
the circuit retains every system Z-readout bit.

Set \delta=t/r andS_2(\delta)=e^{-iA\delta/2}e^{-i\alpha B_0\delta}e^{-iA\delta/2}.

Equations 25/30 of the paper use \lambda=-i\delta and
C=-\alpha\lambda^2[A,B_0]/24. Here[A,B_0]=2i\sum_j a_jb_jY_{2j}Z_{2j+1},\qquad
C=\frac{i\alpha\delta^2}{12}\sum_j a_jb_jY_{2j}Z_{2j+1}.

The implemented complete evolution isV_{\mathrm{CPF}}=e^C S_2(\delta)^r e^{-C}.

The chronological circuit starts with e^{-C} and ends with e^C.
Different pairs commute, so each boundary is a product of exact declared
Pauli rotations. This restricted family needs no approximation to a
commutator exponential. Its gates still use binary64 angles and later need
synthesis and physical error accounting.

The paper’s perturbative local residual has the form
O(\alpha^2|\delta|^3+\alpha|\delta|^5) with model-dependent constants.
At fixed nonzero \alpha, this remains generally second order globally.
Small-\alpha prefactor improvements require comparable unscaled norms.
Here \|A\|=\sum_j|a_j| and \|B_0\|=\sum_j|b_j|; the ledger records their
ratio, including undefined cases when A=0. The saved study reports both
methods’ errors; no universal CPF improvement or fourth-order claim follows
from this finite pair model.

Original Gaussian filtered-jump access, a restricted finite weak reset
channel, finite weighted-decay block access and a one-spin correction block

A Gibbs sampler drives a system toward the mixed state \rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).

Frequency filters weight energy-changing proposals, while the quantum
generator’s detailed balance fixes the thermal stationary state. A fresh
environment records the proposed transition and is then discarded/reset;
this turns a unitary system–environment circuit into a channel on the system.
Stationarity and the number of rounds needed to approach it are separate
questions. Our finite example makes both the transition construction and
its residual Gibbs error visible.

The 2025 Efficient quantum thermal simulation construction uses Gaussian operator-Fourier filters and a corrective coherent term to obtain a synthetic Lindbladian satisfying exact KMS detailed balance. Under the paper’s normalized jump-access condition \|\sum_a(A^a)^2\|\leq1, evolution for time t\geq1 uses signed and controlled Hamiltonian simulation with total time \widetilde O(\beta t); preparation still requires the problem’s mixing time 

Chen et al., 2025.

Exact stationarity of the mathematical generator and accuracy of a finite digital circuit are separate statements. Discretizing filters, truncating local patches, synthesizing rotations and simulating the channel consume their own error budget. Unique stationarity does not establish rapid convergence. The high-temperature results specify regimes in which mixing is provably efficient

Rouzé et al., 2026.

quasilocal KMS generator to overlapping Hamiltonian patches, sample
short-time local channels, and compile their dilations into local circuits

assume local finite-range lattice Hamiltonians and the stated jump-generator
conditions. Approximating the full Gibbs state and estimating a local
observable have different truncation-radius requirements; a fixed small
patch does not establish global accuracy at every system size.

coherent correction,

and Pauli proposals. Each filtered block has a fixed computational-basis
permutation multiplied by diagonal coefficients. Therefore the decay operator

Generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) interleaves general single-qubit
rotations with a unitary signal controlled by one ancilla. Interference creates
a complex polynomial of the signal, including both even and odd powers.
Motlagh and Wiebe establish the polynomial-pair characterization for this
mechanism 

Motlagh & Wiebe, 2024. Our first circuit supplies the angles and
constructs the resulting polynomial; it does not solve the inverse problem
of finding angles for a requested function.

The explicit signal isW_n=e^{i\chi}\left(\prod_{j=0}^{n-2}\mathrm{CZ}_{j,j+1}\right)
\left(\bigotimes_{j=0}^{n-1}R_Z(2z_j)R_Y(2y_j)\right).

Every data wire has actual rotations. The entangling layer has actual gates;
no dense matrix or symbolic oracle is appended. This family is a unitary
signal example, with its own size parameter. It is not an implementation of
the evolution of an arbitrary specified Hamiltonian.

Ancilla q0 is the least-significant wire, and data wire j occupies q(j+1).
The signal operation isD(W)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes W+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes I.

The implementation uses the determinant-one Euler conventionE_j=R_Z(\phi_j)R_Y(2\theta_j)R_Z(\lambda_j).

Chronological gates are E_0,D,E_1,\ldots,D,E_d, hence
V=E_dD\cdots E_1DE_0. For
E_j=\begin{pmatrix}a_j&b_j\\c_j&d_j\end{pmatrix}, ascending-power
coefficient vectors obeyP_0=a_0,\quad Q_0=c_0,\qquad
P_j(z)=a_jzP_{j-1}(z)+b_jQ_{j-1}(z),\quad
Q_j(z)=c_jzP_{j-1}(z)+d_jQ_{j-1}(z).

The source therefore constructs first-column blocks P(W),Q(W) of degree
at most d. Unitarity gives the ideal real-parameter identity
|P(z)|^2+|Q(z)|^2=1 on |z|=1. The numerical checks evaluate selected
points and do not constitute a uniform floating-point certificate.

=e^{i((\phi+\lambda)/2+\pi)}

The

materializes n=2,3,4 at a common output contract. It keeps J=0.6,

one final \langle Z_0\rangle, measured from a complete fresh-input trial;
all other system and environment outcomes are ignored. This local-output task
has a constant score range and a different measurement budget from the total
energy task above.

The step count is chosen from an analytic bound before inspecting numerical
errors. Use the trace norm on Hermitian matrices and its induced map norm.
Hamiltonian commutators have norm at most 2\|H\|_\infty (operator norm), and a standard-GKSL local
lowering dissipator has norm at most 2\gamma_j. A component envelope isA_n=2(n-1)|J|+2n|h_x|+2\sum_j\gamma_j.

Here F(s) is the literal reduced-system channel palindrome after environment
discard, not the joint dilation unitary whose small-time angle has square-root
behavior. Each component has total weight one, so F'(0)=G=\sum_c\mathcal L_c;
palindrome symmetry gives F''(0)=G^2. Every positive-time component
exponential is CPTP and contractive. The product-rule multinomial expansion
gives \|F'''(s)\|\leq A_n^3. The exact channel E(s) has the same third
derivative bound, and palindrome symmetry makes their derivatives through
order two agree at zero. Applying both integral Taylor remainders and then
telescoping the r contractive steps yields\|F(t/r)^r(\rho)-e^{t\mathcal L}(\rho)\|_1
 \leq B_n(r)=\min\!\left(2,\frac{(A_nt)^3}{3r^2}\right).

This is a uniform exact-arithmetic, exact-substep evolution bound for all
input density operators under the stated time-independent positive-time model.
It excludes preparation faults, angle rounding, coherent synthesis and physical
faults. It is a conservative original derivation for this schedule, not an
imported Liouvillian commutator constant or a formal/Lean proof. The literature
provides the surrounding method context 

Strang, 1968

Kliesch et al., 2012.

bounded by B_n/2.

def local_marginal(state,q):
    # Independent explicit partial trace in little-endian three-system order.
    result=np.zeros((2,2),dtype=complex)
    rest=[j for j in range(3) if j!=q]
    for a in range(2):
        for b in range(2):
            for x in range(4):
                offset=sum(((x>>k)&1)<<j for k,j in enumerate(rest))
                result[a,b]+=state[offset|(a<<q),offset|(b<<q)]
    return result

A product formula approximates time evolution by short local rotations. QSP instead treats a Hamiltonian eigenvalue as a signal: for H|v\rangle=E|v\rangle, let x=E/\alpha and \alpha=\sum_j|h_j|. Since |x|\le1, the access circuit and a zero-label reflection preserve a two-dimensional subspace with signal matrixB_x=\begin{pmatrix}x&\sqrt{1-x^2}\\\sqrt{1-x^2}&-x\end{pmatrix}.

The qubitization walk (2\Pi-I)B rotates this subspace through eigenphases \pm\arccos x. Phase rotations interleaved with access calls interfere so that the accepted component becomes a chosen bounded polynomial in x, applied to every eigencomponent without computing eigenvectors

Gilyén et al., 2019.

Here \Pi=|0\rangle\langle0|_{\rm label}\otimes I_{\rm system} andD(\phi)=e^{i\phi(2\Pi-I)},\qquad
V=D(\phi_0)B D(\phi_1)\cdots B D(\phi_d).

The scalar implementation multiplies matrices in this written order. Circuit gates are applied chronologically in reverse phase order, beginning with \phi_d. records.content:
Forward interaction with a qubit bath offers a small environment register:
choose a system coupling and bath frequency, prepare the bath, evolve the
joint system, then discard and reset the bath. Ding, Zhan, Preskill and Lin
analyze this approach for thermal and ground-state preparation


Ding et al., 2026. Here the coupling is an actual local X
operator on a sampled site, and the source expands every forward operation
into visible gates. Increasing the system size changes the Hamiltonian and
the emitted register and gates.

The paper’s end-to-end guarantees depend on its access normalization,
temperature or spectral-gap assumptions and mixing conditions. Its stated
thermal mixing examples include noninteracting spins and quadratic fermions
at \beta=\Theta(1), and a separate result for local commuting systems at
high temperature 

Ding et al., 2026. The diagonal chain
below is local and commuting, but that class membership does not establish
the paper’s normalization, high-temperature or mixing hypotheses for this
particular pulse and sampler. No theorem is reproduced here. The finite
channel may retain bias relative to the Gibbs or ground target, even when
its circuit implementation agrees with the independent reference.

records.content:
Use n system spins indexed from j=0 and one reusable bath qubit E at
wire index n. With \hbar=1, define the open chainH_S^{(n)}=\frac12\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}h_jZ_j
+J\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}Z_jZ_{j+1},\qquad
h_j=1+\frac{j\bmod 3}{8},\qquad J=\frac18,H_E(\omega)=-\frac{\omega Z_E}{2},\qquad
H_{a,\omega}(t)=H_S^{(n)}+H_E(\omega)+g(t)X_aX_E,
\qquad g(t)=0.08e^{-2(t-1)^2},\quad 0\le t\le2.

Every round chooses a uniform site a\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\} and a fresh
frequency from the analytic GL3 law representing uniform density 1/2 on
[0,2]:(\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2)
=\left(1-\sqrt{\frac35},\ 1,\ 1+\sqrt{\frac35}\right),
\qquad (w_0,w_1,w_2)=\left(\frac5{18},\frac49,\frac5{18}\right).

Thermal mode fixes \beta=1 and samples the bath bit with
p_1(\omega)=1/(1+e^\omega). Ground mode always uses bath |0\rangle.
All n+1 qubits are initially reset to zero; an explicit X on E prepares a
sampled bath one. Each round ends with an unobserved bath discard/reset,
including the last round. Terminal measurements map system q_j to output
bit c_j in Z. There is no bath measurement or postselection.

The output contract is the system state, its individual Z expectations and
the final computational-basis distribution after K rounds. For the finite
L-step round unitary U_{a,r,L}, the averaged channel is\Phi_{n,m,L}(\rho)=\frac1n\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}\sum_{r=0}^{2}w_r
\sum_{b=0}^{1}p_m(b\mid\omega_r)
\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[
U_{a,r,L}(\rho\otimes|b\rangle\langle b|)U_{a,r,L}^{\dagger}\right].

Fresh independent choices in the modeled preparation give
\Phi_{n,m,L}^{K}(|0\cdots0\rangle\langle0\cdots0|).
A fixed seeded schedule instead gives its conditional sequence of channels.
Those are distinct objects, and a recorded schedule is not an experimental
population or a purification of the averaged output.

The scheduler uses Python’s random.Random(MT19937) with choice
order site, frequency, then thermal bath bit. It records K logical site
calls and K frequency calls, plus K thermal bit calls. A site call is made
even at n=1; ground mode makes no bath-bit call. These count the public
randrange/random calls, without counting internal generator words or
measuring classical controller time. The emitter consumes recorded choices
and draws no randomness.

Set \hbar=1 and use one system qubit S and one bath qubit E:H_S=\frac{Z_S}{2},\qquad H_E(\omega)=-\frac{\omega Z_E}{2},\qquad
H_\omega(t)=H_S+H_E(\omega)+0.08 f(t)X_SX_E,f(t)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{(t-8)^2}{8}\right],\qquad 0\leq t\leq16.

The finite Gaussian has center 8 and width \sigma=2. The coupling law is
a point mass at A_S=X: this restricted example draws no random coupling
operator. It retains the full XX interaction. In the mathematical basis
|s,e\rangle, its even and odd parity sectors areH_{\mathrm{even}}(t)=\frac{1-\omega}{2}Z+0.08f(t)X
\quad\text{on }\{|00\rangle,|11\rangle\},H_{\mathrm{odd}}(t)=\frac{1+\omega}{2}Z+0.08f(t)X
\quad\text{on }\{|01\rangle,|10\rangle\}.

Both transitions are present, including the counter-rotating sector. The
source therefore does not replace XX by an energy-exchange-only interaction.

Every round draws a new frequency from the 17-point Gauss–Legendre law on
[0,2], whose weights represent the uniform density 1/2. All 17 nodes
contribute to the channel; the resonant node \omega=1 is only one of them.
Thermal mode uses \beta=1 and prepares the bath bit with probabilityp_1(\omega)=\frac{1}{1+e^\omega},\qquad
\rho_E(\omega)=\operatorname{diag}(1-p_1,p_1).

An initial reset prepares E in |0\rangle, and an explicit X gate prepares
|1\rangle when the sampled bit is one. Ground mode always uses bath
|0\rangle. Each round ends with an unobserved bath discard/reset to zero.
After K=192 fresh-draw rounds, the system is measured in Z. The system
starts in |0\rangle, the excited state of H_S; its ground state is
|1\rangle.

For a one-round unitary U_\omega and quadrature weights w_j, the finite
averaged channel is\Phi(\rho)=\sum_j w_j\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[
U_{\omega_j}\bigl(\rho\otimes\rho_E(\omega_j)\bigr)
U_{\omega_j}^{\dagger}\right].

Fresh independent choices every round give \Phi^{192}(\rho), rather than
an average of fixed-frequency channel powers. The saved deterministic
schedules use PCG64 with seed 20261113 and separate thermal/ground
streams. Those records audit the draws; they do not establish statistical
independence of a physical trial population.

records.content:
A symmetric product formula cancels leading splitting errors. Higher-order Suzuki formulas compose several symmetric steps, including backward-evolution steps, to cancel more terms. Extra cancellation can reduce approximation error while adding gates and longer absolute evolution demand. The useful choice depends on the requested accuracy and complete compiled workload 

Childs et al., 2021

Childs et al., 2018.

Evidence and task contract

The canonical 36-case study and all eight notebook code cells have executed in the locked environment. The focused source and release checks passed (119 tests). A separate 32-wire, order-six circuit was generated without dense simulation. The study uses one fixed family, time, initial state and output before comparing orders. Physical projections, certified rotation synthesis and formalization remain planned.

Split an open-chain Hamiltonian into commuting groups,H=A+B,\qquad A=J\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}Z_jZ_{j+1}+h_Z\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}Z_j,
\qquad B=h_X\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}X_j.

Terms within A commute, as do terms within B. Coefficients are real; this implementation explicitly supports ZZ/Z/X chains, not arbitrary complex-weight Pauli lists. Couplings, time and basis inputs are declared before construction. There is no Hamiltonian or time rescaling; \hbar=1 and the Pauli coefficient norm is\lambda=|J|(n-1)+n(|h_X|+|h_Z|).

The chronological base step applies A/2, then B, then A/2:S_2(\delta)=e^{-iA\delta/2}e^{-iB\delta}e^{-iA\delta/2}.

For k\ge2, setp_k=\frac1{4-4^{1/(2k-1)}},\qquad
S_{2k}(\delta)=S_{2k-2}(p_k\delta)^2
S_{2k-2}((1-4p_k)\delta)S_{2k-2}(p_k\delta)^2.

Repeat the full composition r times at \delta=t/r. Orders two, four and six use respectively 1, 5 and 25 Strang blocks per macro-step. At positive time, orders four and six have one and eight negative leaves. Two nested negative factors produce a positive leaf; each actual sign remains in the exported circuit.

A diagonal-half ZZ term uses CX; RZ(J*delta); CX, a diagonal-half Z term uses RZ(hZ*delta), and a full X term uses RX(2*hX*delta). Both diagonal halves and every forward/backward block are materialized; adjacent halves are deliberately left unmerged for transparent source accounting. No dense evolution gate or opaque oracle enters our generator.

Each complete measured trial resets all system wires, prepares the declared computational basis state with X gates, runs the entire recursion and measures every wire in Z. Intermediate source negative durations are instructions for inverse evolution. Their gates still consume positive hardware time.

For a fixed finite Hamiltonian and the ideal exact coefficients, the order-2k global splitting error has the form O(|t|^{2k+1}/r^{2k}), with Hamiltonian/commutator-dependent constants. Those constants and the appropriate output norm matter when choosing r 

Childs et al., 2021. A fitted slope on three spins is not a generic step-selection certificate.

The implementation interprets decimal/rational inputs as exact fractions. It encloses the cube/fifth root of four with 160 exact dyadic bisections and selects each binary64 recursive coefficient from the rational enclosure midpoint. The coefficient error is carried through signed interval multiplication. Actual binary64 leaf weights need not sum exactly to one: the ledger retains their exact rational signed sum and consistency defect instead of silently renormalizing them.

A thermal filter can fail postselection even when its accepted state is accurate. The 

noncommuting thermal-filter circuit supplies an actual preparation unitary, its inverse and a recognizable success pattern. These ingredients let us amplify a known prepared input without changing the accepted thermal state. The experiment below checks that preservation, counts the extra access and reflections, and shows why a higher one-attempt success rate need not give a cheaper workload.

Implementation status

Known-input amplitude amplification is implemented with explicit full-register and label-register reflections. The one-qubit Bell-plus-filter example is checked for rounds 0–4, including negative global signs and full coherent source/primitive equivalence. Complete measured trials include initialization, label readout, reference reset and separate X/Z measurements. Degree and temperature bias remain unchanged. Adaptive/fixed-point amplification, certified synthesis, fault-tolerant physical estimates and a Lean proof remain planned.

Use the same noncommuting model and units as the thermal-filter page:H/E_0=0.6Z+0.4X,\qquad E_0=1,\qquad k_B=1.

The default has \beta=1.25/E_0, Taylor degree K=6 and one system qubit. A second case uses \beta=2/E_0 to expose overrotation. The requested state is \rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}); the measured task estimates its energy from separate X and Z means.

Let n be the number of system qubits, with another n reference qubits. The filter polynomial has an explicit Pauli representationT_K(H)=\sum_{k=0}^K\frac{(-\beta H/2)^k}{k!}=\sum_{j=0}^{L_K-1}b_jP_j,

normalization s=\sum_j|b_j|, m=\lceil\log_2L_K\rceil label qubits and N=2n+m total wires. Zero padding is used in the label register. The default aggregate has three Pauli terms, so n=1, m=2 and N=4.

The actual source circuit A starts from |0_N\rangle, prepares the Bell purification |\Phi_{2^n}\rangle with H and CX gates, and applies explicit PREPARE/SELECT/inverse-PREPARE access. Its success projector is\Pi_f=I_{S,R}\otimes|0_m\rangle\langle0_m|.

The accepted purification has direction (T_K\otimes I_R)|\Phi_{2^n}\rangle and reduced system state\rho_K=\frac{T_KT_K^\dagger}{\operatorname{Tr}(T_K^\dagger T_K)}.

All-zero input preparation is repeatable. No classical eigenvectors or dense exponential are loaded into a quantum gate. The classical matrix answers are small independent references. Pauli coefficient aggregation remains a potentially exponential preprocessing step.

Write the output of A asA|0_N\rangle=\sqrt p\,|g\rangle+\sqrt{1-p}\,|b\rangle,

where |g\rangle is the normalized successful purification and |b\rangle lies outside the zero-label subspace. The two reflections are different:S_f=I-2\Pi_f,\qquad S_0=I-2|0_N\rangle\langle0_N|.

S_f touches only the labels. S_0 touches every input wire, including the system and reference. Applying A S_0 A^\dagger reflects about the actual prepared state. Combining this reflection with S_f rotates the two-dimensional plane spanned by |g\rangle and |b\rangle 

Brassard et al., 2002.

Both reflections use X gates to turn their zero pattern into an all-one pattern, followed by an H–MCX–H multi-controlled Z and X gates to undo the conversion. An empty success register gives S_f=-I, recorded as a global phase. There is no dense reflection gate.

Starting with A, each chronological round is S_f,A^\dagger,S_0,A, plus the required global \pi phase:Q=-A S_0 A^\dagger S_f,\qquad A_r=Q^r A.

Why the thermal preparation needs this reflection

records.content:
Oblivious amplification leaves an unknown system input outside its initial reflection and uses an ancilla-only projector on both sides. For a nonunitary filter, that construction generally reshapes its unequal singular values and changes the thermal eigenweights 

Berry et al., 2014

Berry et al., 2015.

A bounded contrast replaces the full S_0 here by the labels-only S_f. For the default one-round case, the resulting reduced state is about 0.8133 in trace distance from the original polynomial state. The correct known-input construction preserves it to numerical precision. These are different algorithmic contracts: the known Bell input makes the full-input reflection available, without a reflection about an unknown state or quantum cloning.

Implemented choices on this page are unamplified preparation (r=0), fixed integer known-input amplification and the explicitly labeled ancilla-only contrast. Fixed-point/phase-adjusted schedules, efficient estimation of unknown success, scalable thermal-access constructions and physical comparisons remain planned.

r full-input reflections on N=2n+m wires and r success reflections on m labels;

Each full source call includes the Bell gates and one PREPARE/SELECT/inverse-PREPARE access. Its inverse is an actual inverse circuit. The source preparation and access are counted on all 2r+1 calls; initialization and final readout are charged once per complete attempt. There are no intermediate resets or early-abort savings.

This bounded example implements a noncommuting imaginary-time Taylor filter with actual PREPARE/SELECT/unprepare access. Its conditional purification and reduced thermal state are checked against independent matrix-polynomial and Gibbs references. Full reset/readout attempts and capped retries are counted. The separate

A conditional physical-resource study below supplies actual Clifford+T compilation for the unamplified degree-6 X/Z task. Classical Pauli aggregation can be exponential; unrestricted Gibbs methods, certified synthesis and hardware calibration remain planned.

The 

thermal spectral-filter variant now uses generated QSP phases and direct Hamiltonian access across explicit sizes and inverse temperatures. It avoids this example’s Pauli-power aggregation, while retaining bounded phase generation and materialization limits. Let c_j,t be the stated rational coefficients and time, c_j^{(b)} their recorded binary64 values interpreted exactly, and \delta_b the binary64 segment duration. The helper chooses the smallest r\le32 for whichx=\sum_j|c_j^{(b)}|\,|\delta_b|\le\tfrac12,

then the smallest degree K\le8 meeting the algorithm-bias allowance. This is a bounded selection rule, not a global circuit-cost optimization. For H_b=\sum_jc_j^{(b)}P_j, the exact exposure correction\eta_{\rm model}=\sum_j|r\delta_b c_j^{(b)}-t c_j|

bounds \|e^{-ir\delta_bH_b}-e^{-itH}\| by the Hermitian unitary Duhamel bound. It corrects the coefficient/time model only; it does not bound probability, angle or lowering arithmetic.

Define T=\sum_{k=0}^K(-i\delta_bH_b)^k/k! and s_K=\sum_{k=0}^K x^k/k!. The geometric majorant\tau=\frac{x^{K+1}/(K+1)!}{1-x/(K+2)},\qquad s_K\le2

bounds the Taylor remainder uniformly over |\lambda|\le\sum_j|c_j^{(b)}|, without subtracting approximate exponentials or inferring accuracy from one input. The next omitted term ratio is at most x/(K+2).

For native access, let D_0=(1+\tau)^r-1. The comparison bound is\|T^r-e^{-itH}\|\le D_{\rm native}=D_0+\eta_{\rm model},\qquad
p_{\min}\ge\left(\frac{1-D_0}{s_K^r}\right)^2\quad(D_0<1).

The accepted map is T^r/s_K^r. Its attenuation is included in acceptance and retries; the reported operator comparison concerns the unscaled T^r, not a claim that the attenuated map is close to e^{-itH}.

The normalization-two label refers to the pre-amplification source block T/2. After one OAA round, the accepted segment isB=\frac{3T-TT^\dagger T}{2}.

Writing T=U_\delta(I+F) for U_\delta=e^{-i\delta_bH_b}, \|F\|\le\tau, the linear perturbation is (F-F^\dagger)/2. Three quadratic terms and one cubic term give\|B-U_\delta\|\le E=\tau\left(1+\tfrac32\tau+\tfrac12\tau^2\right).

Since the ideal accepted block is a contraction, \|B\|\le1, composition gives\|B^r-e^{-itH}\|\le D_{\rm padded}=rE+\eta_{\rm model},\qquad
p_{\min}\ge(1-E)^{2r}\quad(E<1).

The nonlinear B does not retain a fixed normalization-two interpretation and still has rejection and polynomial bias. For either mode, D<1 gives the conservative conditional unit-norm-Pauli bias bound 4D/(1-D); the chosen K is the smallest candidate satisfying 4D/(1-D)\le\epsilon/5. Unsafe candidates receive no positive acceptance bound by squaring a negative amplitude. The downloads retain exact fractions, using lossless hexadecimal integer strings for very large records; decimal values are presentation only.
